blocks.text: INNWS -Wacana who tries to place Soeharto as a national hero is often built with social memory theories that heroism can be selective and periodic. Such an approach seems intellectual, but fails to touch the core of Indonesian history. Our problem is not in a way of remembering, it's in the way that countries fail to sever the power networks that make up those wounds. 1998's reform never completed its primary task because the structure of the New Order was never dismantled; it was only moved to the corner, while still alive.

When the old government fell, there was no filter on his political architects. The political party that became the main instrument of the regime remained intact and was soon back to becoming a great player. The central figures who have been at the core of power have never been removed from the arena. The economic networks that they build are still operating with old patterns, just changing faces. Even the family that became a symbol of its previous era's power still has space and political resources not small. In short, the old foundation stays firm, while the state structure just changes the paint.

Therefore nostalgia against the New Order does not arise as a pure sense of society, but as a result of the work of networks that still have an interest in maintaining that old image. When actors of the previous era still control the stage of communication and political resources, it's only natural that old narratives seem relevant. It's not a historical longing; it's the success of strategy forming perception.

Some analysts blame the Reformation characters for failing to build new symbols and narratives. But any narrative will be difficult to survive when the entire state mechanism is still powered by the hands raised by the former system. Reform is not a failure because of the idea, but because it never breaks the machine that it wants to replace. How is it possible that a new idea can win when all political infrastructure is still under the influence of the once dominant group in those days?

In a context like this, an approach that assesses historical figures based on their heroic phase of history becomes irrelevant. Social memory theory can be used for figures who live in a moral dilemma or ethical struggle, but cannot be applied to regimes that systematically oppress their people. Washington or Mandela got a positive assessment not because they closed their eyes on the historical premonitions, but because of their contributions to stand up for the struggle for the liberation of his nation. Not with a political system that has spent decades constructing fear and injustice.

If today there's a urge to put Soeharto as a hero, it's not a sign of nation manhood in history. It's a sign that the political powers that once ruled the country were back in space. In reading history, the problem is not looking at glass half full or half empty, but seeing who's holding it. And to this day, the influence of the core group of the old regime is still very strong in determining the course of the nation.

Indonesia does not require the bleaching of history, but it is the courage to admit that reform has yet to touch the root of its problem. As long as the New Order's legacy party remains a power shaft, during the previous era's political network is still controlling national resources, and as long as families are in the center of power remain main players, then the reformation narrative will always be established.

Soeharto is not a national hero. He was only a hero to those who still enjoy the benefits of the structure he left behind. For the Indonesian people, it's still an unfinished homework. And as long as the job hasn't been done, reform will continue to be a half-baked story, left alive by those who never really wanted change.
